name: Keeping Financial Data Out of Public Models
title: Keeping Financial Data Out of Public Models
answer: Keeping financial data out of public models concerns the controls, policies, and technical measures that prevent proprietary or regulated financial information from being used in training or fine-tuning publicly accessible AI models. This includes customer account data, transaction records, internal pricing models, and material non-public information held by banks, asset managers, insurers, and corporate finance teams. The scope also covers indirect exposure through third-party vendors, shared cloud workspaces, and employee use of consumer AI tools. For the AI Accountant, this topic sits at the boundary of data governance, model risk, and regulatory compliance.

sections.body: Keeping financial data out of public models concerns the controls, policies, and technical measures that prevent proprietary or regulated financial information from being used in training or fine-tuning publicly accessible AI models. This includes customer account data, transaction records, internal pricing models, and material non-public information held by banks, asset managers, insurers, and corporate finance teams. The scope also covers indirect exposure through third-party vendors, shared cloud workspaces, and employee use of consumer AI tools. For the AI Accountant, this topic sits at the boundary of data governance, model risk, and regulatory compliance.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of data loss prevention tools, egress filtering, model access controls, and audit logging systems. Organizations typically deploy these controls at the network perimeter, on managed endpoints, and inside cloud environments where financial data is stored or processed. Public model interfaces, including consumer chatbots and hosted API endpoints, are treated as untrusted destinations unless explicitly approved. The infrastructure also includes identity and access management systems that tie model usage to individual employee accounts and data classification tags.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners begin by mapping where financial data lives and how it flows, then classify records by sensitivity and regulatory status. They block or redact high-risk fields before any prompt or upload can reach a public model, using pattern matching, named entity recognition, and policy-based filters. For approved use cases, they may use synthetic data, aggregated summaries, or locally hosted models so that raw financial values never leave the controlled environment. Ongoing work includes reviewing prompt logs, testing for accidental leakage, and updating rules when new data types or model features appear.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main rights and risks concern confidentiality, regulatory exposure, and the loss of trade secrets or client trust. Financial data is often subject to legal duties such as bank secrecy, data protection law, and market abuse rules, so an accidental disclosure into a public model can create compliance findings or litigation risk. Provenance matters because once data enters a public model, it may be retained, used for further training, or surfaced in outputs to other users, and the original owner may have little ability to retract it. Governance therefore relies on clear ownership, documented approval paths, and evidence that controls were active at the time of any model interaction.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward tighter default blocking, more granular data classification, and greater use of private or on-premises model deployments for financial work. Regulators and auditors are beginning to ask firms to show how they prevent public model leakage, which will push controls from ad hoc blocks into formal model risk frameworks. At the same time, model providers are adding enterprise data controls and contractual terms that address training use, but firms still need to verify those terms against their own data obligations. Over time, the boundary between public and private models may become more automated, with real-time redaction and policy enforcement built into the tools themselves.
